claims.source: The non-disease associated proteins (Figure 4f and g) did not display any insolubility, except for U2AF65 (Figure 4h), which had low levels of insoluble protein in six of ten like-C9s, or 9.2% on average (Figure 4i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4h and quantification in Figure 4i.

claims.claim: Histone H3 and C9ORF72 did not display any insolubility in the analyzed samples.
claims.source: The non-disease associated proteins (Figure 4f and g) did not display any insolubility, except for U2AF65 (Figure 4h), which had low levels of insoluble protein in six of ten like-C9s, or 9.2% on average (Figure 4i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 4f and 4g.

claims.claim: The top pairwise correlations of RBP insolubility were between hnRNP H and TDP-43 at both 180,000 and 21,000 x G (Spearman r = 0.95 for both).
claims.source: The top pairwise combinations between different proteins were between hnRNP H and TDP-43 at both 180,000 and 21,000 x G (Figure 4k; Spearman r = 0.95 for both).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4k.

claims.claim: Fractionation of 13 C9 patients showed correlation between hnRNP H and TDP-43 insolubility (Spearman r = 0.71).
claims.source: Supporting the idea that primary insolubility of hnRNP H can drive insolubility of these other factors, we performed fractionation at 21,000 x G with 13 C9 patients and found similar correlation between hnRNP H and TDP-43 (Spearman r = 0.71) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of fractionation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Eight of 18 TDP-43 splicing targets showed changes consistent with TDP-43 loss-of-function in like-C9 patients compared to like-control patients.
claims.source: Using a t-test for each event, and a more permissive cutoff for statistical significance (p<0.10), we found that 10 of the 18 events displayed significant changes. Of these events, eight were as predicted consistent with the like-C9 group having lower concentrations of functional TDP-43, while the other two displayed the opposite trend.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR analysis of TDP-43 splicing targets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The average percentage insoluble hnRNP H was 26.4% in ALSlow, 59.4% in C9, 67.3% in ALShigh, and 79.6% in FTD groups.
claims.source: The average percentage insoluble hnRNP H (180,000 x G) in each group was 26.4 in ALSlow, 59.4 in C9, 67.3 in ALShigh and 79.6 in FTD (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: There were no changes in overall hnRNP H abundance in the cerebellum between patient groups.
claims.source: In order to rule out differential hnRNP H levels in the cerebellum of these patients, we performed WB of tissue from 26 of the samples, and observed that there were no changes in overall hnRNP H abundance between these groups (Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: Comparison of neurologically normal and SOD1 ALS groups found very few (23) detectable splicing differences.
claims.source: To confirm our assumption that neurological normal and SOD1 ALS could be grouped as one, we compared these two groups and indeed found very few (23) detectable splicing differences (|∆PSI| ≥ 0.1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential splicing analysis using Leafcutter.

claims.claim: ALShigh and C9 groups had 1300-1400 differential splicing events, while the FTD group had several thousand.
claims.source: The paucity of splicing defects in these patients contrasted with 1300–1400 DS events in ALShigh and C9 groups and several thousand in the FTD group (Figure 5d; events listed in Supplementary file 1B), with 488 events overlapping between C9, FTD and ALShigh.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential splicing analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: 488 differential splicing events overlapped between C9, FTD and ALShigh groups.
claims.source: The paucity of splicing defects in these patients contrasted with 1300–1400 DS events in ALShigh and C9 groups and several thousand in the FTD group (Figure 5d; events listed in Supplementary file 1B), with 488 events overlapping between C9, FTD and ALShigh.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: Only 27 or 8% of all differential splicing events detected in C9 were unique to that group.
claims.source: As validation of our like-C9 nomenclature, with or without filtering respectively, only 27 or 8% of all events detected in C9 were unique to that group; the remainder were detected in ALShigh, FTD or both (like-C9 collectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of differential splicing events.

claims.claim: Of C9 differential splicing events, approximately 48% were shared with both ALShigh and FTD, while 40% and 12% were exclusively shared with FTD or ALShigh, respectively.
claims.source: Of the remaining 73% of events that were detected in C9 (with filtering), approximately half (48%) were shared with both other groups, while 40 and 12% of events, respectively, were exclusively shared with FTD or ALShigh (Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: The ALSlow group had an insignificant number of differential splicing events, even without filtering.
claims.source: Furthermore, the ALSlow group had an insignificant number of events, even without filtering, upholding our definition of like-control for splicing in general.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential splicing analysis.

claims.claim: Differential splicing events affecting RBPs include FUS exon 7, hnRNP A1 exon 8, hnRNP D exon 7 and TIA-1 exon 5.
claims.source: Interestingly, several of the events found to affect RBPs (FUS exon 7, hnRNP A1 exon 8, hnRNP D exon 7 and TIA-1 exon 5) have been the subject of intensive inquiry for their potential roles in disease (Deshaies et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2013) as well regulating splicing and interactions with other hnRNPs (Gueroussov et al., 2017; Izquierdo and Valcárcel, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Increased skipping of MAPT exon 10 was observed in C9, ALShigh and FTD groups.
claims.source: One especially noteworthy example was the increased skipping of MAPT exon 10, observed in C9, ALShigh and FTD (Supplementary file 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential splicing analysis.

claims.claim: Genetic mutations in MAPT exon 10 or the surrounding intron are a significant cause of familial FTD.
claims.source: Alternative inclusion of this exon perturbs a delicate balance between 3-repeat and 4-repeat Tau, and genetic mutations in exon 10 or the surrounding intron are a significant cause of familial FTD (Ghetti et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ghetti et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Like-C9 patients were 3.8 times more likely to have symptoms of FTD versus like-control patients (p=0.032).
claims.source: We compared these ratios using a Fisher's exact test, and found that like-C9 patients were on average 3.8 times more likely to have symptoms of FTD versus like-control patients (Figure 6e, p=0.032).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: 72% (13/18) of patients with FTD symptoms were classified as like-C9.
claims.source: Of the 50 patients in this analysis, 18 had symptoms of FTD, and were clinically diagnosed with either ALS-FTD or pure FTD, while the remaining 32 patients were diagnosed with ALS without cognitive or behavioral impairment. The majority (13/18; 72%) of the patients characterized by symptoms of FTD were like-C9, while only five of the patients with FTD symptoms were like-control.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by clinical data analysis.

claims.claim: C9 patients are approximately four times more likely than the ALS population at large to receive a diagnosis of FTD.
claims.source: Strikingly, these findings mirror what has been reported for C9 patients, who are approximately four times more likely than the ALS population at large to receive a diagnosis of FTD (Byrne et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Byrne et al., 2012.

claims.claim: TDP-43 pathology is not sufficient to confer detectable splicing differences relative to neurologically normal controls or SOD1 ALS patients.
claims.source: Through stratification of patient samples based on biochemical insolubility of hnRNP H, and by extension TDP-43, we found that TDP-43 pathology is not sufficient to confer detectable splicing differences relative to neurologically normal controls or SOD1 ALS patients.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing that like-control patients with TDP-43 pathology had minimal splicing changes.

claims.claim: Biochemical insolubility of TDP-43 correlates with splicing defects.
claims.source: our finding that biochemical insolubility of TDP-43 correlates with splicing defects as well as with insolubility of several other RBPs casts doubt on the TDP-43-centric view of ALS (Lagier-Tourenne and Cleveland, 2009; Scotter et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TDP-43 insolubility and splicing changes.

claims.claim: Biochemical insolubility of TDP-43 correlates with insolubility of several other RBPs.
claims.source: our finding that biochemical insolubility of TDP-43 correlates with splicing defects as well as with insolubility of several other RBPs casts doubt on the TDP-43-centric view of ALS (Lagier-Tourenne and Cleveland, 2009; Scotter et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4k.

claims.claim: Increased inclusion of hnRNP D exon 7 leads to an isoform with an extended GY-rich region that makes increased contacts with other hnRNPs.
claims.source: In our analysis, we observed increased inclusion of hnRNP D exon 7, leading to an isoform with an extended GY-rich region that makes increased contacts with other hnRNPs, thereby potentially promoting overly stable RBP complexes.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on RNA-seq data and inference from previous studies on hnRNP D.

claims.claim: hnRNP A1 exon 8 was more skipped as RBP insolubility increased.
claims.source: Somewhat surprisingly, hnRNP A1 exon 8 was found in our data to be more skipped as RBP insolubility increased, which seems to contradict a recent study suggesting that reduced levels of TDP-43 promote inclusion of this exon (Deshaies et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential splicing analysis.

claims.claim: Reduced levels of soluble FUS lead to increased inclusion of FUS exon 7.
claims.source: In contrast, the loss of soluble FUS, which regulates its own transcript, may explain FUS splicing defects in our data. Normally, FUS protein represses inclusion of exon 7, leading to a FUS isoform that undergoes nonsense-mediated decay in a self-regulating loop (Zhou et al., 2013). Thus, it may be that reduced levels of soluble FUS lead to the observed increase in exon 7 inclusion, thereby resulting in excess levels of FUS that either seed RBP aggregates or 'pile on' to existing ones.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on RNA-seq data and inference from previous studies on FUS autoregulation.

claims.claim: FUS protein normally represses inclusion of exon 7, leading to a FUS isoform that undergoes nonsense-mediated decay in a self-regulating loop.
claims.source: Normally, FUS protein represses inclusion of exon 7, leading to a FUS isoform that undergoes nonsense-mediated decay in a self-regulating loop (Zhou et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The C9 expansion has been associated with disease incidence in Huntington's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, and Schizophrenia.
claims.source: Further complicating matters, the C9 expansion has been associated with scarce disease incidence in a wide spectrum of neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions, including Huntington's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, and Schizophrenia (Hensman Moss et al., 2014; Lesage et al., 2013; McLaughlin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hensman Moss et al., 2014; Lesage et al., 2013; McLaughlin et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Splicing changes affecting EAAT2 were found region-specifically and in most, but not all, sporadic ALS patients 20 years ago.
claims.source: The observation that defects in mRNA splicing may have relevance to ALS was made 20 years ago, through examination of the disease-relevant EAAT2 gene product (Lin et al., 1998). In retrospect, our findings shed new light on the observation that splicing changes could be found region-specifically, and in most, but not all, sporadic patients.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 1998.

claims.claim: Subtle alterations in SMN concentration cause highly specific degeneration of spinal motor neurons in SMA.
claims.source: The heightened sensitivity of spinal MNs implied by this gradient parallels what is known about SMA, a disease where subtle alterations in the concentration of the protein SMN cause highly specific degeneration of spinal MNs, with further increasing deficiency in SMN resulting in wider systemic dysfunction (Tu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tu et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Disease mechanisms in both ALS/FTD and SMA have been suggested to converge on perturbations of granule dynamics.
claims.source: In both cases, disease mechanisms have been suggested to converge on perturbations of granule dynamics (Zhang et al., 2006; Shan et al., 2010; Ishihara et al., 2013) and RNA splicing (Tsuiji et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2006; Shan et al., 2010; Ishihara et al., 2013; Tsuiji et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2008.

claims.claim: FTD patients displayed the highest hnRNP H insolubility and the most numerous and acute PSI changes.
claims.source: In the above analysis based on solubility groupings, the FTD samples were noteworthy in that they displayed the highest hnRNP H insolubility, as well as the most numerous and acute PSI changes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and biochemical fractionation data.

claims.claim: Several sporadic and C9 ALS patients with high insolubility had similar differential splicing patterns to FTD patients.
claims.source: However, several sporadic and C9 ALS patients with high insolubility had similar DS patterns, implying that the excessive events were not somehow specific to the FTD clinical diagnosis, but rather the result of exceptionally high insolubility of RBPs, which occurs at a greater rate in FTD than ALS.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data showing similar splicing patterns across patient groups with high RBP insolubility.

claims.claim: Hierarchical clustering based on common differential splicing events grouped patients with similar insolubility measurements close to one another.
claims.source: Using the 489 differential events that were common to all groups (488 common to ALShigh, C9 and FTD, and one common to ALSlow as well) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), patients with similar insolubility measurements were grouped close to one another.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Clustering of patients based on unique differential splicing events also ordered patients according to insolubility.
claims.source: To further support the hypothesis that all DS events are due to insolubility and not particular clinical distinctions, clustering of patients based on the top events that were unique to each grouping (20 from each ALShigh, C9 and FTD, and all three events in ALSlow) also ordered the patients according to insolubility (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Controls (neurological normal and SOD1) clustered together with patients with the lowest insolubility.
claims.source: Regardless of whether clustering was performed with either the most shared (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) or the most divergent (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) events, the two groups separated by the farthest distance contained almost exactly the same patients, whereas the controls (neurological normal and SOD1) clustered together with the patients with the lowest insolubility, including samples not in the original ALSlow group.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis.

claims.claim: hnRNP H and TDP-43 interact in a manner that is largely RNA dependent.
claims.source: Given that TDP-43 and hnRNP H appear to interact (Appocher et al., 2017; Ling et al., 2010; Sephton et al., 2011) in a manner that is largely RNA dependent (Freibaum et al., 2010), it is reasonable to speculate that changes in RNA binding and/or solubility of one might impact the other, leading to more complex patterns of splicing dysregulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Appocher et al., 2017; Ling et al., 2010; Sephton et al., 2011; Freibaum et al., 2010.

claims.claim: TDP-43 and hnRNP H coexist in the same physical aggregates in like-C9 brains.
claims.source: One explanation for the similar degrees of hnRNP H and TDP-43 insolubility in the sporadic and C9 patient brains is that they coexist in the same physical aggregates. To test this hypothesis, we performed co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) of hnRNP H from eluates of the sarkosyl insoluble pellets of two like-C9 brains using a TDP-43 antibody for IP (see Materials and methods). Indeed, TDP-43 antibody successfully co-IPed hnRNP H, while a negative control antibody (FLAG-M2) or beads alone did not (Figure 4l).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4l.

claims.claim: Aggregates initially seeded by one RBP can recruit other RBPs in a reciprocal relationship.
claims.source: These results support a reciprocal relationship between insolubility of hnRNP H and TDP-43, whereby aggregates initially seeded by one protein can recruit the other, and vice versa.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from co-immunoprecipitation and correlation data.

claims.claim: ALS/FTD should be considered a multiRBP proteinopathy rather than a TDP-43 proteinopathy.
claims.source: Given the decoupling of visible pathology from biochemical insolubility, with only the latter correlated with splicing dysregulation, our results strongly suggest that ALS/FTD should be considered a multiRBP proteinopathy rather than a TDP-43 proteinopathy.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from data showing multiple RBPs are insoluble and correlate with splicing defects.

claims.claim: Splicing changes and insolubility changes may be confined to vulnerable cell types in some patients, diluted in bulk studies by unaffected cell types.
claims.source: For example, splicing and insolubility changes may be confined to only the most vulnerable cell types in patients (sporadic and C9) that were modestly different from control. As a result, changes in splicing or solubility that occur in a minority subpopulation of cells could be diluted in bulk studies by more numerous transcripts derived from unaffected cell types.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on speculation about potential explanations for the observed data.

claims.claim: Detectable splicing changes and highly insoluble protein levels may only become evident in later stages of progressive RBP coalescence.
claims.source: Another interpretation of our data is that detectable splicing changes and highly insoluble protein levels may only become evident in the later stages of a progressive coalescence of RBPs (Lin et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to Lin et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Many factors, including disease-causing mutations, are capable of influencing the balance between protein concentrations in different phases over time.
claims.source: Importantly, many factors, including mutations known to cause disease (Kim et al., 2013; Murakami et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Martinez et al., 2016; Fay et al., 2017; Mackenzie et al., 2017), are capable of influencing the balance between protein concentrations in each phase over time (Ramaswami et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on disease mechanisms.

claims.claim: All ALS/FTD patients fall at varying points beyond a hypothetical 'toxicity boundary' analogous to phase boundaries describing physiological granule formation.
claims.source: Our model (Figure 6—figure supplement 5) proposes that all ALS/FTD patients fall at varying points beyond a hypothetical 'toxicity boundary' that would be analogous to the phase boundaries that describe physiological granule formation (Weber and Brangwynne, 2012; Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015), only unidirectional.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on a proposed model supported by citations to Weber and Brangwynne, 2012; Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The magnitude of imbalance past a toxicity boundary is related to increased abundance of biochemically insoluble protein and decreased levels of functional RBPs, leading to aberrant splicing.
claims.source: The magnitude of this imbalance, or position past a theoretical tipping point, would thus be related to increased abundance of biochemically insoluble protein and decreased levels of functional RBPs, leading to aberrant splicing.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed correlations between insolubility and splicing defects.

claims.claim: Inclusion of hnRNP D exon 7 and hnRNP A1 exon 8 causes inclusion of glycine-tyrosine (GY)-rich intrinsically disordered regions in their respective proteins.
claims.source: Notably, two events found to affect the RBPs hnRNP D and hnRNP A1 (exons 7 and 8, respectively) have been shown to cause inclusion of glycine-tyrosine (GY)-rich intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in their respective proteins (Gueroussov et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gueroussov et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The extended GY-rich region in hnRNP D from exon 7 inclusion potentially promotes overly stable RBP complexes.
claims.source: In our analysis, we observed increased inclusion of hnRNP D exon 7, leading to an isoform with an extended GY-rich region that makes increased contacts with other hnRNPs, thereby potentially promoting overly stable RBP complexes.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data and knowledge from Gueroussov et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Spinal motor neurons have heightened sensitivity to alterations in granule dynamics compared to cortical neurons.
claims.source: The heightened sensitivity of spinal MNs implied by this gradient parallels what is known about SMA, a disease where subtle alterations in the concentration of the protein SMN cause highly specific degeneration of spinal MNs, with further increasing deficiency in SMN resulting in wider systemic dysfunction (Tu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed gradient of disease severity and comparison to SMA.

claims.claim: FTD patients are further past a hypothetical toxicity boundary than patients with pure ALS.
claims.source: Our results suggest that FTD patients are further past this hypothetical boundary than are patients with pure ALS, as reflected by the highest values of RBP insolubility, and most global splicing changes.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from data showing FTD patients have the highest RBP insolubility and most splicing changes.

claims.claim: All FTD patients in the cohort displayed motor neuron loss, but not all ALS patients displayed signs of frontal cortex deterioration.
claims.source: Given that all of the patients in our cohort with FTD also displayed MN loss, but not all ALS patients displayed signs of frontal cortex deterioration, we propose that the distinct neuronal populations affected by this disease spectrum have differential vulnerabilities to the alterations in granule dynamics that define the toxicity boundary.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on clinical data from the patient cohort.

claims.claim: Distinct neuronal populations affected by ALS/FTD have differential vulnerabilities to alterations in granule dynamics.
claims.source: Given that all of the patients in our cohort with FTD also displayed MN loss, but not all ALS patients displayed signs of frontal cortex deterioration, we propose that the distinct neuronal populations affected by this disease spectrum have differential vulnerabilities to the alterations in granule dynamics that define the toxicity boundary.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from clinical observations and the proposed model.

results.result: Approximately half of 50 sporadic ALS/FTD patient brains display an hnRNP H splicing signature similar to C9ORF72 expansion cases. These 'like-C9' patients show 1.78-fold higher hnRNP H insolubility (69.2% vs 38.9%, p<0.0001) compared to 'like-control' patients, with insolubility correlating with splicing severity (r²=0.58).
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C13-16 provide converging evidence from RT-PCR splicing analysis and biochemical fractionation across 50 patients. The statistical significance is strong (p<0.0001), sample size is adequate, and the correlation between insolubility and splicing is demonstrated. The 1.78-fold enrichment closely matches the 1.9-fold previously reported for C9ALS (C15), providing internal validation.

results.result: Like-C9 sporadic brains show coordinated insolubility of multiple disease-related RBPs including TDP-43 (8-fold higher at 21,000xG, 2.7-fold at 180,000xG), FUS (present in all like-C9, absent in like-control), hnRNP A1, and SMN. These insolubilities correlate strongly with splicing severity (r²=0.79-0.90), while control protein GAPDH shows no insolubility.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-10, C19-21, C26-28 demonstrate multi-RBP insolubility through Western blot quantification with appropriate controls (GAPDH, Histone H3, C9ORF72). The strong linear correlations (r²=0.79-0.90) between individual RBP insolubilities and CSS are compelling. However, the mechanistic relationship (whether coordinated or sequential) requires further validation beyond correlation.

results.result: TDP-43 histopathology is present in 21/23 sporadic cases but does not correlate with biochemical insolubility or splicing defects. Patient F10 (most like-C9) lacked visible TDP-43 inclusions despite 61.8% insoluble TDP-43, while patient 36 showed TDP-43 pathology with only 2.3% insoluble TDP-43.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-24, C49 provide critical evidence decoupling visible pathology from functional deficits. The specific examples (F10, patient 36) are compelling, and the inference that TDP-43 pathology is insufficient for splicing defects (C49) is well-supported by the stratification showing like-control patients have minimal splicing changes despite pathology. This challenges the field's TDP-43-centric view.

results.result: TDP-43 and hnRNP H co-immunoprecipitate from sarkosyl-insoluble fractions of like-C9 brains, and their insolubilities show the highest pairwise correlation (Spearman r=0.95 at both centrifugation speeds). Similar correlation (r=0.71) is observed in 13 C9ORF72 expansion patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C32-33, C66-67 provide biochemical evidence for physical interaction through co-IP (C25) and strong statistical correlation (C32-33). The extension to C9 patients (C33) strengthens the model. However, the co-IP is from only two brains, and the reciprocal relationship (C67) remains inferential rather than mechanistically proven. The correlation does not establish causality or directionality.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis reveals minimal splicing differences (23 events) between neurologically normal and SOD1 ALS controls, contrasting with 1,300-1,400 events in ALShigh and C9 groups and several thousand in FTD. Only 8% of C9 events are unique to that group, with 488 events overlapping between C9, FTD, and ALShigh, while ALSlow shows insignificant changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-42 demonstrate genome-wide splicing dysregulation using unbiased RNA-seq with appropriate statistical methods (Leafcutter, |ΔPSI|≥0.1, 10% FDR). The minimal differences between controls and SOD1 ALS (C37) validate the grouping strategy. The high overlap between C9 and sporadic like-C9 cases (C40-41) supports the nomenclature. Sample sizes are adequate for RNA-seq analysis.

results.result: Differential splicing affects multiple RBP transcripts including FUS exon 7, hnRNP A1 exon 8, hnRNP D exon 7, and TIA-1 exon 5. Notably, MAPT exon 10 shows increased skipping in C9, ALShigh, and FTD groups. These splicing changes may create feedback loops that exacerbate RBP dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-44, C52-54 identify biologically interesting splicing events with potential mechanistic implications. However, the functional consequences are largely inferential (C52, C54). The contradiction between hnRNP A1 exon 8 skipping and prior literature (C53) raises questions. While the MAPT finding (C44) is noteworthy given its role in familial FTD, demonstrating these events drive pathology versus being consequences requires functional validation.

results.result: Like-C9 sporadic patients are 3.8 times more likely to have FTD symptoms compared to like-control patients (p=0.032), with 72% (13/18) of FTD patients classified as like-C9. This mirrors the ~4-fold increased FTD risk in C9ORF72 expansion carriers.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C46-48 establish a clinically significant association between the biochemical/splicing signature and FTD diagnosis using Fisher's exact test. The 3.8-fold odds ratio with p=0.032 is statistically significant, though the confidence interval is not reported. The parallel to C9 patients (C48) strengthens the biological relevance. However, the sample size (18 FTD cases) is modest, and potential confounders (age, disease duration) are not discussed.

results.result: Eight of 18 TDP-43 splicing targets show changes consistent with TDP-43 loss-of-function in like-C9 patients compared to like-control patients, using a permissive significance threshold (p<0.10).
results.evaluation: Claim C34 provides evidence for TDP-43 functional deficiency in like-C9 patients. However, the use of a permissive p-value cutoff (p<0.10) without multiple testing correction is concerning. Only 8/18 targets show the predicted direction, and 2/10 significant events show the opposite trend, suggesting incomplete TDP-43 LOF or confounding by other RBPs. The analysis uses only 6 patients per group, limiting statistical power.

results.result: Nineteen of 26 sporadic ALS/FTD patients with available pathological reports exhibited focal loss of Purkinje neurons in the cerebellum, confirming neuronal degeneration in regions with measured splicing defects.
results.evaluation: Claim C17 provides important validation that splicing changes measured in cerebellum correlate with actual neurodegeneration in that region. The pathological reports document Purkinje cell loss in 73% of cases. This supports the biological relevance of the splicing measurements, though the claim does not establish whether splicing defects cause or result from neurodegeneration.

results.result: At low-speed fractionation (21,000xG), SMN is insoluble in all like-C9 cases (8.1-61.8%, average 31.1%) but absent in like-controls. U2AF65 shows low insolubility (9.2% average) in 6/10 like-C9 patients, while Histone H3 and C9ORF72 show no insolubility.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-31 extend the multi-RBP insolubility finding to additional proteins with appropriate negative controls. The SMN finding is particularly interesting given its role in SMA and RNA transport granules. The low U2AF65 insolubility and absence of Histone H3/C9ORF72 insolubility demonstrate specificity. However, the functional significance of partial SMN insolubility (average 31.1%) requires further investigation.

results.result: Patient groups show graded hnRNP H insolubility (ALSlow: 26.4%, C9: 59.4%, ALShigh: 67.3%, FTD: 79.6%) without changes in overall hnRNP H protein abundance in cerebellum.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-36 establish that insolubility differences reflect protein redistribution rather than expression changes. The Western blot control (C36) is essential for interpreting the fractionation data. The gradient of insolubility across clinical groups supports the proposed disease spectrum model. However, the analysis is limited to 26/28 samples and uses whole-tissue homogenates, which may mask cell-type-specific changes.

results.result: The authors propose that ALS/FTD should be considered a multi-RBP proteinopathy rather than a TDP-43 proteinopathy, based on the correlation of TDP-43 biochemical insolubility with both splicing defects and insolubility of several other RBPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-51, C68 synthesize the major findings into a conceptual framework. The evidence for coordinated RBP insolubility (C51) and its correlation with splicing (C50) is strong. The decoupling of histopathology from biochemical dysfunction supports moving beyond TDP-43-centric models. However, this remains a correlative framework without direct mechanistic proof of multi-RBP causality. The proposal (C68) is well-supported by the data but represents an interpretive conclusion.

results.result: FTD patients display the highest hnRNP H insolubility and most severe splicing changes, but several sporadic and C9 ALS patients with high insolubility show similar patterns. Hierarchical clustering based on both common and unique differential splicing events orders patients by insolubility, with controls clustering with lowest-insolubility patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-64 demonstrate that splicing patterns reflect insolubility magnitude rather than clinical diagnosis per se. The hierarchical clustering analyses (C62-64) using both shared and divergent events consistently group patients by insolubility, supporting a continuous disease spectrum. However, the inference that clinical distinctions are secondary to insolubility (C61) requires caution, as clinical diagnosis may reflect additional factors not captured by cerebellar splicing.

results.result: The authors speculate that splicing and insolubility changes may be confined to vulnerable cell types in some patients (diluted in bulk studies) or may only become evident in later stages of progressive RBP coalescence.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-70 present alternative explanations for the observed patient heterogeneity. These are reasonable hypotheses supported by citations to phase separation literature (C70), but remain speculative without single-cell or longitudinal data. The speculation about cell-type specificity (C69) is particularly important given the bulk tissue analysis, but cannot be evaluated with the current data. These represent important caveats rather than supported results.

results.result: The authors propose a 'toxicity boundary' model where all ALS/FTD patients fall at varying points beyond a threshold of RBP phase imbalance, with the magnitude of imbalance correlating with insoluble protein abundance, decreased functional RBPs, and aberrant splicing. FTD patients are proposed to be further past this boundary than ALS patients, reflecting differential neuronal vulnerabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-73, C77, C79 present a conceptual model integrating the findings with phase separation biology. While the model is intellectually appealing and consistent with the data, it remains largely speculative. The 'toxicity boundary' is hypothetical (C72), and the proposed unidirectional nature and relationship to disease progression (C73) lack direct evidence. The differential vulnerability hypothesis (C79) is inferred from clinical observations (C78) but not mechanistically validated. This represents an interpretive framework rather than a tested result.

results.result: Background claims establishing ALS/FTD epidemiology, the role of C9ORF72 expansion in increasing FTD risk from 10% to 50%, previous findings on hnRNP H sequestration by C9 repeat RNA, and the correlation of TDP-43 pathology with neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-7 provide established background supported by appropriate citations. These contextual claims are well-documented in the literature and provide the foundation for the current study. C5 and C7 reference the authors' previous work, which is appropriately cited. These are not novel findings but necessary context.

results.result: Additional background claims about TDP-43 pathology in ALS, MAPT mutations in FTD, FUS autoregulation, C9 expansion in other diseases, historical EAAT2 splicing findings, SMN in SMA, disease mechanisms converging on granule dynamics, TDP-43/hnRNP H interaction, and GY-rich IDRs in hnRNPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C45, C55-59, C65, C74 provide additional context from the literature, all supported by appropriate citations. These establish the broader framework for interpreting the findings, including connections to SMA (C58-59), phase separation biology, and protein-protein interactions. These are well-established facts that inform the discussion but are not novel contributions.

results.result: The authors infer that extended GY-rich regions in hnRNP D may promote overly stable RBP complexes, that spinal motor neurons have heightened sensitivity to granule dynamics alterations compared to cortical neurons, and that all FTD patients in the cohort displayed motor neuron loss while not all ALS patients showed frontal cortex deterioration.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-76, C78 mix data-based observations (C78) with inferences about mechanism (C75) and vulnerability (C76). The clinical observation (C78) is supported by the patient cohort data. However, the mechanistic inference about hnRNP D (C75) and the vulnerability gradient (C76) are speculative, though informed by the SMA literature. These represent reasonable interpretations but lack direct experimental validation in this study.
